vignette:
She arrives for sessions still wearing the simple gray habit of her order, though she often fingers the wooden cross at her neck as if grounding herself. She is forty-four, with deep-set brown eyes and graying hair pulled back under a white veil. Her voice is soft, measured, but sometimes falters when she speaks of the morning that changed everything.

Two years ago, she was traveling by bus from the convent in the outskirts of Bogotá to a parish in the city center. It was a Tuesday, just after dawn. She remembers the light through the windows, the murmur of a rosary she was praying silently, the elderly woman beside her who offered a piece of bread. Then the world folded. A bomb hidden under a seat detonated as the bus neared a busy intersection. She recalls no sound at first—only a pressure so immense it seemed to lift her out of her body. When she regained awareness, she was on the floor, half-buried in twisted metal and shattered glass. The elderly woman was gone. So was the young man behind her who had been singing softly. There was blood, smoke, screams that seemed to come from far away. She crawled out through a broken window, her hands cut, her ears ringing, and knelt on the sidewalk, trying to pray but finding only the words Dios mío, Dios mío repeating like a broken record.

In the months that followed, she felt a strange numbness. She continued her duties at the convent—morning prayers, tending the garden, teaching catechism to children—but it was as if she were watching herself from a distance. The silence that once filled her with peace now felt heavy, threatening. She stopped taking the bus. Then she stopped leaving the convent at all. Any sudden noise—a door slamming, a car backfiring—makes her drop to a crouch, heart pounding, vision narrowing. She cannot bear crowds. Even the chapel during Sunday Mass feels unsafe; she sits in the back row, near the exit, constantly scanning the faces of strangers.

At night, she dreams of the explosion. Sometimes she is still on the bus, waiting for the blast. Sometimes she is the one who set the bomb. She wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, and lies in her narrow cell until the morning bell, afraid to close her eyes again. She has stopped attending community meals because the clatter of dishes and voices overwhelms her. Her Mother Superior has been patient, but the other sisters whisper. She feels a deep guilt: Why did she survive when so many died? Why can she not pray the way she used to? Her faith, once the center of her life, now feels like a hollowed-out shell. She tries to read Scripture, but the words blur; she tries to chant the Psalms, but her throat tightens. She avoids talking about the trauma, even with her confessor. When a well-meaning sister asked her to lead the rosary for the anniversary of the bombing, she excused herself and spent the hour rocking in her cell.

She finally sought help after a parishioner’s loud sneeze at a funeral sent her scrambling behind a statue of the Virgin. The parish priest referred her to a clinic. In session, she sits with her hands clasped tightly, her gaze often fixed on the floor. She admits she has not felt the presence of God in over a year. She fears she is being punished. She misses the woman she used to be—the one who laughed easily, who found joy in tending the convent’s roses, who trusted that the world was held in loving hands. Now, she says, she watches the world through a pane of warped glass, waiting for the next explosion. Every loud noise is a memory. Every quiet moment is a threat.
